options.A: The denominator effect occurs when alternative asset values fall faster than public asset values.
options.B: The denominator effect refers to fee calculations dividing by committed rather than invested capital.
options.C: The DENOMINATOR EFFECT occurs when the DENOMINATOR of an allocation percentage (total portfolio value) FALLS faster than the NUMERATOR (alt allocation, whose stale/appraisal NAV is unchanged), pushing the alt weight ABOVE policy targets.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The mechanism is the reverse — PUBLIC assets (the denominator) fall faster while lagged private marks hold up.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Fees are unrelated; the effect is the alternative WEIGHT rising passively as total portfolio value shrinks.
rationales.C:
Full statement: the DENOMINATOR EFFECT occurs when the DENOMINATOR of an allocation percentage (total portfolio value) FALLS faster than the NUMERATOR (alt allocation, whose stale/appraisal NAV is unchanged), pushing the alt weight ABOVE policy targets; happened widely in 2008–09 and 2022; investor may be forced to rebalance by SELLING PUBLIC ASSETS (procyclical) or delay rebalancing until alt NAVs remark down; creates unintended concentration.

Correct. Per curriculum §8: the denominator effect is a widely-observed alt-specific risk during market drawdowns.

questions.stem: Funding risk for private equity most likely:

options.A: FUNDING RISK: the risk that an LP cannot meet capital calls when they arrive.
options.B: FUNDING RISK: the risk that the GP fails to deploy committed capital before the fund's term expires. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.C: FUNDING RISK: the risk that distributions arrive faster than the LP can profitably reinvest them.

rationales.A:
Full statement: FUNDING RISK: the risk that an LP cannot meet capital calls when they arrive; typically manifests during liquidity crises when portfolio value is down, spending needs are up, and PE managers accelerate capital calls into distressed opportunities; consequences include DEFAULT (loss of fund interest, distributions), forced selling of liquid assets at unfavorable prices, or borrowing at high cost; managed through commitment pacing, liquidity reserves, and secondary sales.

Correct. Per curriculum: funding risk is a critical alt-specific risk requiring pacing and liquidity planning.
rationales.B: Describes deployment/dry-powder risk on the GP side; funding risk is the LP's inability to meet capital calls.
rationales.C: Confuses funding risk with reinvestment risk; the concern is meeting capital calls, not redeploying distributions.

questions.stem: Key-person risk in alternatives most likely:

options.A: Key-person risk is eliminated in alternatives because large firms rely on standardized, team-based processes. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.B: Many alt strategies depend on a SPECIFIC individual or small team (founder-manager).
options.C: Key-person risk refers to the departure of the LP's chief investment officer from the investing institution.

rationales.A: Understates the exposure; many alt strategies still hinge on a specific founder or small team, which LP key-person provisions exist to address.
rationales.B:
Full statement: many alt strategies depend on a SPECIFIC individual or small team (founder-manager); loss of that key person via departure, death, or dispute can materially impair returns; typically addressed via KEY-PERSON PROVISIONS in LP agreements (right to suspend investment period or terminate fund if key persons cease active involvement); diligence should identify and monitor key persons; concentration in single-manager alt exposures amplifies key-person risk.

Correct. Per curriculum §8: key-person risk is prominent in alts and mitigated through LP agreement provisions and monitoring.
rationales.C: Locates the risk on the wrong side; it concerns loss of the manager's key individuals, not the investor's staff.

questions.stem: Fee drag on net returns for alternatives most likely:

options.A: Fund-of-funds layers eliminate fee drag by negotiating away the underlying managers' carry.
options.B: Typical alt fee structures (2 & 20) can reduce gross returns by 400–600 bps per year.
options.C: Typical alt fee structures reduce gross returns by only 10–20 bps per year, comparable to index funds. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.

rationales.A: Backwards; a fund-of-funds adds another fee layer on top of the underlying managers, increasing total drag.
rationales.B:
Full statement: typical alt fee structures (2 & 20) can reduce gross returns by 400–600 bps per year; combined with FUND-OF-FUNDS layers (additional ~1% + 10%), total fee drag can exceed 700 bps; for alts to justify inclusion, GROSS alpha must exceed the total fee drag PLUS the illiquidity premium demanded; failure to consider net-of-fee returns leads to systematic overallocation.

Correct. Per curriculum: fee drag is material and must be modeled net; FoF layers compound the drag.
rationales.C: Drastically understates fee drag; 2-and-20 structures cost hundreds of basis points annually, not index-fund levels.

questions.stem: Illiquidity budget concept most likely:

options.A: An ILLIQUIDITY BUDGET is the maximum share of the portfolio the investor is willing to hold in illiquid assets, given horizon, spending needs, and stress-testing requirements.
options.B: An illiquidity budget is the minimum allocation to illiquid assets required to fully harvest the illiquidity premium.
options.C: The illiquidity budget is an output of mean-variance optimization, expanding automatically when MVO assigns higher weights to private assets. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.

rationales.A:
Full statement: an ILLIQUIDITY BUDGET is the maximum share of the portfolio the investor is willing to hold in illiquid assets, given horizon, spending needs, and stress-testing requirements; sets a HARD CAP on cumulative allocation to private equity, private credit, direct real estate, and other illiquid alts; used as a policy constraint in AA — even if MVO suggests higher weights, budget prevents unintended illiquidity concentration.

Correct. Per curriculum §8: an illiquidity budget serves as a policy constraint preventing overexposure to illiquid alts.
rationales.B: Incorrect. This inverts the concept — the budget is a CAP, not a floor: it limits the maximum illiquid share consistent with horizon, spending needs, and stress tests rather than mandating a minimum to earn the premium.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The budget is a POLICY CONSTRAINT imposed on the optimization — it binds even when MVO suggests higher illiquid weights, not the reverse.

questions.stem: Concentration risk in alt manager selection most likely:

options.A: CONCENTRATION risk arises when a small number of managers dominate the alt allocation.
options.B: Concentration risk applies only to public equity portfolios, not to alternative manager selection.
options.C: Concentration risk is negligible in alternatives because manager returns are highly correlated with one another.

rationales.A:
Full statement: CONCENTRATION risk arises when a small number of managers dominate the alt allocation; single-manager loss (departure, fraud, poor performance) can drive material portfolio impact; MITIGATION includes: diversifying across multiple managers, capping individual manager exposure (typically <25% of any strategy), diversifying across strategies within an alt category, and vintage-year diversification for private markets.

Correct. Per curriculum: manager concentration is a critical alt-specific risk requiring active diversification.
rationales.B: Manager concentration is a core alt-specific risk mitigated by diversifying across managers, strategies, and vintages.
rationales.C: False premise; wide manager dispersion means single-manager exposure carries substantial idiosyncratic risk, so concentration matters greatly.

questions.stem: Long-horizon investor's ability to capture illiquidity premium most likely:

options.A: Long-horizon investors (endowments, SWFs, young pensions) can capture MORE of the illiquidity premium than short-horizon investors because: (1) they can wait out lockups.
options.B: Investment horizon is unrelated to an investor's ability to harvest the illiquidity premium.
options.C: Short-horizon investors capture more of the illiquidity premium because they trade more frequently. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.

rationales.A:
Full statement: long-horizon investors (endowments, SWFs, young pensions) can capture MORE of the illiquidity premium than short-horizon investors because: (1) they can wait out lockups; (2) they can withstand denominator effects without forced selling; (3) they can allocate across vintages smoothly; (4) they benefit from compounding of premium over longer periods; short-horizon investors face STRUCTURAL disadvantages in alt investing.

Correct. Per curriculum: horizon is the key determinant of the ability to profitably capture the illiquidity premium.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Horizon is the KEY determinant: endowments, SWFs, and young pension plans can wait out lockups and cycles, capturing more of the premium.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Frequent trading is incompatible with illiquid holdings — short horizons force exits at the worst prices.

questions.stem: Illiquid alts' risk profile under stress most likely:

options.A: Reported risk metrics overstate stress-period risk, making illiquid alts appear more dangerous than they are.
options.B: Illiquid alts genuinely reduce portfolio risk under stress because their NAVs decline less than public assets.
options.C: Reported risk METRICS understate stress-period risk because appraisal-based NAVs SMOOTH real economic losses.

rationales.A: Reverses the bias; smoothed data understates, not overstates, true stress-period risk.
rationales.B: Mistakes smoothed appraisal NAVs for real protection; the smaller reported decline is a valuation lag, not genuine risk reduction.
rationales.C:
Full statement: reported risk METRICS understate stress-period risk because appraisal-based NAVs SMOOTH real economic losses; investors face LOSS OF OPTIONALITY (cannot rebalance, cannot access capital for emergency needs); CROSS-DEFAULT and CROSS-COLLATERALIZATION provisions in fund LP agreements can amplify losses; forced sales in secondary markets often occur at 20–40% discounts to reported NAV during stress.

Correct. Per curriculum §9: illiquid alt risk profiles are materially worse in stress than reported metrics suggest.

questions.stem: Secondary-market discounts for LP interests most likely:

options.A: SECONDARY MARKET for LP interests exists but discounts to NAV are typically 5–15% in normal times, expanding to 20–40% during stress.
options.B: No secondary market exists for limited partnership interests.
options.C: LP interests trade in the secondary market at premiums to NAV during market stress. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.

rationales.A:
Full statement: SECONDARY MARKET for LP interests exists but discounts to NAV are typically 5–15% in normal times, expanding to 20–40% during stress; the discount compensates buyers for: DUE DILIGENCE effort, transfer-approval delays, unfunded commitment liability, and buyer market power in a distressed seller environment; secondary sales are a RELEASE VALVE for liquidity but at real cost.

Correct. Per curriculum: secondary market provides liquidity release valve but with meaningful discount cost.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The secondary market exists and has grown large.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Stress moves pricing the other way — discounts of 5-15% in normal times WIDEN to 20-40% under stress.

questions.stem: Gates and side pockets in hedge funds most likely:

options.A: GATES guarantee investors full redemption on demand regardless of the fund's liquidity conditions.
options.B: GATES limit total redemptions per period (e.g., 25% of AUM per quarter) to prevent forced liquidation during crises.
options.C: SIDE POCKETS hold the fund's most liquid positions and are redeemable daily at NAV.

rationales.A: Opposite of a gate's function; gates cap redemptions to prevent fire sales, impairing rather than guaranteeing investor liquidity.
rationales.B:
Full statement: GATES limit total redemptions per period (e.g., 25% of AUM per quarter) to prevent forced liquidation during crises; SIDE POCKETS segregate ILLIQUID or hard-to-value positions from the main fund, with distributions when they are realized; both mechanisms PROTECT the fund from fire sales but IMPAIR investor liquidity precisely when it is most needed; investors must MODEL these mechanisms as part of liquidity planning.

Correct. Per curriculum §9: gates and side pockets are common HF liquidity constraints that need to be considered in AA.
rationales.C: Backwards; side pockets segregate illiquid, hard-to-value positions and pay out only as those assets are realized.

questions.stem: Impact of alt illiquidity on rebalancing most likely:

options.A: Rebalancing is CONSTRAINED for illiquid alts — cannot readily reduce PE exposure without secondary sales at discount.
options.B: Illiquidity has no effect on rebalancing because private NAVs move too little to breach policy bands. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.C: Illiquid alts can be rebalanced as easily as public assets by trimming positions at reported NAV.

rationales.A:
Full statement: rebalancing is CONSTRAINED for illiquid alts — cannot readily reduce PE exposure without secondary sales at discount; upward drift in alt allocations from denominator effect cannot be quickly corrected; rebalancing must primarily use LIQUID components (public equity/bonds); this creates PROCYCLICAL rebalancing behavior (sell public assets after they've fallen) unless investor pre-plans liquidity reserves and rebalancing rules.

Correct. Per curriculum §9: illiquidity constrains rebalancing to liquid components and creates procyclical behavior without planning.
rationales.B: Overlooks the denominator effect, which drives alt weights above target and cannot be quickly corrected due to illiquidity.
rationales.C: Ignores that reducing PE exposure requires secondary sales at a discount, so rebalancing is constrained, not frictionless.

questions.stem: Liquidity tiering approach to portfolio construction most likely:

options.A: Liquidity tiering applies only to the cash and Treasury bill portion of the portfolio.
options.B: Liquidity tiering assigns all portfolio holdings to a single tier based on total portfolio size.
options.C: Assign portfolio holdings to LIQUIDITY TIERS based on how quickly they can be converted to cash: Tier 1 (cash + T-bills, immediate).

rationales.A: Incorrect. Cash and bills are merely Tier 1; the framework spans every holding out to the multi-year illiquid tier, matched against needs.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Tiering is MULTI-level by conversion speed — a single bucket defeats the exercise.
rationales.C:
Full statement: assign portfolio holdings to LIQUIDITY TIERS based on how quickly they can be converted to cash: Tier 1 (cash + T-bills, immediate); Tier 2 (public equity/bonds, days); Tier 3 (hedge funds with quarterly redemptions); Tier 4 (private equity/real estate, years); ensure each tier is sized to meet its respective LIABILITIES and STRESS scenarios; helps prevent liquidity gaps between commitments and available funds.

Correct. Per curriculum §9: liquidity tiering aligns holdings with liability structure and stress needs.

questions.stem: Illiquidity's impact on portfolio construction most likely:

options.A: Illiquidity forces the investor to make INITIAL commitments carefully (cannot easily reverse), plan LIQUIDITY reserves for capital calls and spending, DIVERSIFY across vintages and managers (can't concentrate then rebalance), and accept HIGHER volatility in the effective liquid portfolio (denominator effect during drawdowns).
options.B: Illiquidity has no impact on how alternative allocations should be constructed, since capital calls and distributions net out over the life of a well-diversified fund program. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay. Applied uniformly, it would bind at every horizon and every asset class. No cycle overlay would be allowed to lift or cut that bound.
options.C: Illiquid commitments can be reversed easily and cheaply through the secondary market at NAV, so initial sizing decisions carry little weight and can be corrected at any time.

rationales.A:
Full statement: illiquidity forces the investor to make INITIAL commitments carefully (cannot easily reverse), plan LIQUIDITY reserves for capital calls and spending, DIVERSIFY across vintages and managers (can't concentrate then rebalance), and accept HIGHER volatility in the effective liquid portfolio (denominator effect during drawdowns); the operational implication is a more thoughtful, gradual portfolio-building process vs public-only investing.

Correct. Per curriculum: illiquidity necessitates a different portfolio construction discipline than liquid public-market investing.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Illiquidity reshapes construction — reserves, pacing, and diversification discipline all follow from it.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Reversal is costly (secondary discounts) or impossible; INITIAL commitments must be made carefully, with liquidity reserves planned for capital calls.

questions.stem: Illiquidity in normal markets vs stress markets most likely:

options.A: Illiquidity is constant across market states, so secondary discounts do not change during stress.
options.B: Alt liquidity improves during stress as distressed buyers compete to purchase LP interests.
options.C: In NORMAL markets, secondary markets function and liquidity is available at moderate discounts (5-15%).

rationales.A: Illiquidity is state-dependent; secondary discounts widen sharply and gates activate precisely during stress.
rationales.B: Reverses reality; liquidity deeply contracts in stress, with wider discounts and paused distributions, not improved access.
rationales.C:
Full statement: in NORMAL markets, secondary markets function and liquidity is available at moderate discounts (5-15%); in STRESS markets, liquidity DEEPLY CONTRACTS — secondary discounts widen to 20-40%, gates activate, side pockets are used, and NEW commitments and distributions may pause; the concept of 'illiquidity' is state-dependent — worse when needed most.

Correct. Per curriculum: alt liquidity contracts sharply in market stress, which is when investors most need liquidity.

drills.los_text: discuss considerations in monitoring alternative investment programs

questions.stem: Monitoring alt investments — key focus areas most likely:

options.A: Once due diligence is complete at inception, ongoing monitoring of alt managers adds little value.
options.B: Monitoring is limited to verifying the quarterly NAV statements provided by the fund administrator. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.C: Monitoring covers: (1) PERFORMANCE vs BENCHMARK (PME, IRR, TVPI for PE; index-relative for HF).

rationales.A: Ignores that style drift, key-person changes, and operational red flags emerge over time and require continuous monitoring.
rationales.B: Far too narrow; monitoring spans performance, style drift, key persons, fees, valuation, liquidity, risk, and operational due diligence.
rationales.C:
Full statement: monitoring covers: (1) PERFORMANCE vs BENCHMARK (PME, IRR, TVPI for PE; index-relative for HF); (2) MANAGER FIT — style drift, strategy consistency; (3) KEY-PERSON changes; (4) FEES and expense drag; (5) VALUATION methodology and independence; (6) LIQUIDITY and cash flow — capital call rate, distribution rate; (7) RISK measures — leverage, concentration, factor exposures; (8) OPERATIONAL DUE DILIGENCE — controls, audits, custody.

Correct. Per curriculum §11 monitoring: comprehensive framework spans investment and operational aspects.

questions.stem: Public Market Equivalent (PME) for private equity most likely:

options.A: PME compares private-fund cash flows to a HYPOTHETICAL PUBLIC-INDEX investment with the same call/distribution timing.
options.B: PME compares a private fund's IRR directly to the public index's time-weighted return, ignoring cash-flow timing. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.C: PME measures a private fund's gross-of-fee return against its own prior-quarter reported NAV.

rationales.A:
Full statement: PME compares private-fund cash flows to a HYPOTHETICAL PUBLIC-INDEX investment with the same call/distribution timing; a PME above 1.0 indicates PE outperformed the public benchmark; PME accounts for TIMING of cash flows (unlike simple IRR comparisons) and represents the ILLIQUIDITY PREMIUM captured; widely used to evaluate PE managers against public alternatives.

Correct. Per curriculum §11 PME: standard benchmark for PE that adjusts for cash-flow timing.
rationales.B: Misses the essence of PME, which replicates the fund's actual call and distribution timing rather than comparing headline IRRs.
rationales.C: Wrong benchmark; PME measures net cash flows against a hypothetical public-index investment, not against the fund's own lagged NAV.

questions.stem: Style drift in hedge funds most likely:

options.A: Style drift is the natural evolution of markets and requires no monitoring response.
options.B: STYLE DRIFT: a manager deviates from the stated strategy — e.g., an equity market-neutral fund taking directional bets, or a distressed-debt fund allocating to growth equity.
options.C: Style drift refers to a fund's returns drifting below its benchmark over consecutive quarters. Underperformance is a results problem; drift is a PROCESS problem — deviation from the stated strategy.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Drift is a monitoring red flag: a market-neutral fund taking directional bets changes the investor's risk without consent.
rationales.B:
Full statement: STYLE DRIFT: a manager deviates from the stated strategy — e.g., an equity market-neutral fund taking directional bets, or a distressed-debt fund allocating to growth equity; drift can be intentional (manager pursuing perceived opportunity) or unintentional (accumulated positions); monitoring detects drift via: consistency of factor exposures, sector concentration, gross/net exposure, portfolio characteristics; drift may trigger a REDEMPTION or manager REVIEW.

Correct. Per curriculum §11 style drift: significant monitoring dimension in HF investing.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Underperformance is a results problem; drift is a PROCESS problem — deviation from the stated strategy.

questions.stem: Operational due diligence (ODD) most likely:

options.A: ODD is a one-time legal review of the LP agreement completed before the initial commitment.
options.B: ODD examines NON-INVESTMENT risks: valuation policies and independence of pricing sources.
options.C: ODD focuses on forecasting the manager's future investment returns and alpha generation.

rationales.A: Understates ODD; it is an ongoing review of operational controls across custody, audit, valuation, and personnel, not a single legal check.
rationales.B:
Full statement: ODD examines NON-INVESTMENT risks: valuation policies and independence of pricing sources; custody arrangements; audit firms and audit history; regulatory registrations and history; internal controls and segregation of duties; personnel background checks; disaster recovery; business continuity; ODD failures are LEADING causes of hedge fund fraud losses (Madoff, others), so ODD often carries VETO authority in institutional programs.

Correct. Per curriculum §11 ODD: distinct from investment DD; often the source of critical red flags.
rationales.C: Confuses ODD with investment due diligence; ODD assesses non-investment risks like valuation, custody, audit, and controls.

questions.stem: IRR limitations as PE performance metric most likely:

options.A: IRR: (1) assumes REINVESTMENT at the IRR itself, often unrealistic.
options.B: IRR assumes reinvestment at the risk-free rate, understating a successful fund's true return. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.C: IRR is a complete performance measure requiring no supplementation by TVPI, DPI, or PME.

rationales.A:
Full statement: IRR: (1) assumes REINVESTMENT at the IRR itself, often unrealistic; (2) can be MANIPULATED by early distributions (e.g., quick partial exits); (3) doesn't reflect absolute value creation (TVPI does); (4) VINTAGE-SPECIFIC — cannot be compared across dissimilar time periods without adjustment; (5) doesn't compare to public alternative (PME does); good practice uses IRR alongside TVPI, DPI, and PME.

Correct. Per curriculum: IRR is one metric but should not be used in isolation.
rationales.B: Wrong assumption and direction; IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself, which tends to overstate, not understate, returns.
rationales.C: IRR alone is insufficient; it must be paired with TVPI, DPI, and PME because of its reinvestment and manipulation limitations.

questions.stem: Cumulative vintage exposure monitoring most likely:

options.A: Concentrate all commitments in a single vintage year to simplify tracking and reporting.
options.B: Monitor CUMULATIVE COMMITMENT and DEPLOYED CAPITAL by VINTAGE YEAR to detect over- or under-commitment vs pacing plan.
options.C: Vintage-year tracking becomes unnecessary once the target private-market allocation is first reached.

rationales.A: Single-vintage concentration creates cyclical timing risk; the goal is deploying across vintages to smooth exposure.
rationales.B:
Full statement: monitor CUMULATIVE COMMITMENT and DEPLOYED CAPITAL by VINTAGE YEAR to detect over- or under-commitment vs pacing plan; VINTAGE CONCENTRATION creates cyclical risk; ideally, deploy across multiple vintages to smooth returns; if under-committing in a year, may need to CATCH UP via secondaries or larger primary commitments; monitoring both current and future committed capital allows dynamic pacing.

Correct. Per curriculum: vintage-year monitoring supports smooth deployment and diversified exposure.
rationales.C: Ongoing pacing is required to maintain the target against distributions and NAV changes, so vintage monitoring continues past the initial target.

questions.stem: Manager benchmark selection for hedge funds most likely:

options.A: Hedge funds are best benchmarked against a public equity index such as the S&P 500 regardless of strategy.
options.B: A single broad hedge fund index is an unbiased, precise benchmark for any individual strategy.
options.C: HF benchmark selection is CHALLENGING because indices are HETEROGENEOUS and SUFFER FROM BIASES.

rationales.A: An equity index ignores each strategy's distinct exposures; benchmarking should be strategy-specific and supplemented with absolute measures.
rationales.B: Broad indices are heterogeneous and bias-laden; strategy-specific benchmarks and peer groups are needed instead.
rationales.C:
Full statement: HF benchmark selection is CHALLENGING because indices are HETEROGENEOUS and SUFFER FROM BIASES; STRATEGY-SPECIFIC benchmarks preferred (e.g., HFRI equity market neutral); consider PEER GROUPS with similar strategy and risk profile; ABSOLUTE benchmarks (like cash + 400 bps) provide clarity but ignore market environments; combining PEER-RELATIVE and ABSOLUTE benchmarks provides more comprehensive evaluation.

Correct. Per curriculum: HF benchmarking requires strategy-specific indices supplemented by absolute measures.

questions.stem: Alt program monitoring frequency and depth most likely:

options.A: A single annual review cycle is sufficient for the entire alternatives program.
options.B: Monitoring should be MULTI-FREQUENCY: quarterly performance/attribution/fee review at fund level.
options.C: Event-driven reviews should replace all scheduled monitoring, triggered only by manager news. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.

rationales.A: Too infrequent; monitoring must be multi-frequency, combining quarterly, monthly, annual, and event-driven reviews.
rationales.B:
Full statement: monitoring should be MULTI-FREQUENCY: quarterly performance/attribution/fee review at fund level; annual comprehensive review including ODD refresh; monthly liquidity/exposure aggregation across program; event-driven review on key-person changes, style drift signals, or performance outliers; portfolio-level reviews annually against strategic objectives; systematic monitoring PREVENTS surprises.

Correct. Per curriculum: alt monitoring should span multiple frequencies and depths of review.
rationales.C: Event-driven review supplements but cannot replace regular scheduled performance, liquidity, and operational reviews.
